target.thesis: Where output-time facts underdetermine whether a remark was an assertion (blurts, confabulations, and possibly chatbot outputs), the speaker's later owning or disowning helps settle which act was performed. Determinate cases are fixed at utterance.
target.headline: Whether a chatbot output is an assertion is not settled at the time of output by the system's states or functions; it is conferred by what the system later does with the output, so the same token string can be an assertion or a non-assertion depending on its continuation.
target.target: The shared synchronic assumption in Williams and Bayne, Gubelmann, and Butlin and Viebahn that speech-act status depends on states of the producer at the time of output.
target.sketch: Every position in the debate, including Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion, treats speech-act status as a synchronic property fixed by the producer at the moment of production. Intentions, descriptive function, sanctionability and proxy relations are all evaluated at output time. The counterexample is the human case of retroactive ownership. A speaker blurts out a claim without having formed any intention to commit, such as a half-conscious remark or a confabulated explanation. Challenged, they say 'yes, I stand by that', defend it, and retract it when refuted. We rightly say they asserted it, and that they were answerable for it from the start. So the premise that the act is fixed by pre-utterance mental or functional states is false even for humans. Commitment-management after the fact (defending, retracting, updating on challenge) is at least partly constitutive. On this picture the proto-assertion question becomes diachronic and testable. In a long-context or agentic loop, a model that defends, corrects or retracts an earlier output under challenge confers assertoric status on that output, and a one-shot completion never does. The key premise is that retroactive ownership is constitutive of the act rather than merely evidence of an earlier intention.

findings.part: Later conduct by the producer or interlocutor helps fix which act an earlier utterance was (general claim, not specific to blurts or LLMs)
findings.source: Roulet (apparently; author not shown in the result), "Speech act theory and the analysis of conversation", book chapter, ResearchGate listing, undated
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="44-6">A reactive move in conversation can retroactively give an interpretation to the initiative move.</cite> <cite index="44-9">The sequencing retroactively defines the initiative move's degree of contextual appropriateness.</cite>
findings.note: Discourse analysis already holds that later moves retroactively interpret earlier ones, but about interpretation and appropriateness, not assertoric commitment, blurts or confabulation. I could not check authorship or the full text.

findings.part: The act-type of a prior turn is settled partly in the producer's own later (third-position) turn
findings.source: "Action Ascription in Social Interaction" (conversation-analytic work), ResearchGate listing, c. 2022
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="40-10">Intersubjectivity is taken to be accomplished only if the producer of the first action produces a turn in third position.</cite> <cite index="40-9">The next turn alone shows only the recipient's understanding of the prior action.</cite>
findings.note: This is close to 'the speaker's later owning helps settle the act', but it is framed as an epistemic or analytic warrant (a proof procedure), not as constitutive of the act. That gap is where the thesis's key premise sits.

findings.part: Next-turn evidence of the act performed (the evidential reading of retroactive ownership)
findings.source: "Action categorization in Conversation Analysis and Interactional Linguistics: Challenges and perspectives", Research on Language and Social Interaction, 2026
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="45-2">Whether an action has been recognized as intended becomes observable through the response in the next turn.</cite>
findings.note: It supplies the 'later conduct is mere evidence' rival to the constitutive premise, which a referee will raise.

findings.part: The proto-assertion question as diachronic, turning on commitments incurred and retracted across a human–LLM exchange
findings.source: "Talking with Language Models" (authors not shown in the result), arXiv 2610.09064, 2026
findings.what_they_say: The paper offers a 'Diachronic Argument' about the <cite index="68-13">conversational scoreboard</cite>. It asks whether a <cite index="68-9">persisting interlocutor</cite> bears commitments, meaning the entity to whom retractions, challenges and enforcements are directed.
findings.note: The diachronic framing for LLM assertion already exists. It is used to deny LLM assertion, and it is about a commitment-bearer, not about retroactive ownership fixing the act.

findings.part: LLM extension: a model that defends or retracts an earlier output confers assertoric status on it
findings.source: "Talking with Language Models" (authors not shown in the result), arXiv 2610.09064, 2026
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="68-4">Users edit outputs, discard them, and request alternatives without treating the first attempt as a commitment to be withdrawn.</cite> <cite index="68-11">Even a persisting virtual instance yields only quasi-commitment.</cite>
findings.note: It argues that the loop behaviour the thesis relies on does not generate real commitment. The thesis must say why a model's defending or retracting is ownership and not interpretable-as-ownership.

findings.part: Retroactive ownership as constitutive of the act, since the past act is fixed
findings.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Speech Acts" (discussing Sbisà 2007)
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="30-8">Nothing done on Wednesday can change the fact that an assertion or promise was made on Monday.</cite> Later retraction <cite index="30-10">releases one from the commitments in spite of the fact that the past is fixed.</cite>
findings.note: The standard view makes later retraction a new act that discharges commitment and leaves the earlier act's identity untouched. The thesis must either narrow to underdetermined cases or deny this.

findings.part: Defending and retracting as the commitment-management that characterises assertion
findings.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Assertion" (Spring 2024 ed.); Marsili, "The definition of assertion: Commitment and truth", Mind & Language, 2024
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="60-3,60-4">Asserting commits one to providing grounds in response to challenge, and one escapes the commitment only by withdrawing the assertion.</cite> Marsili likewise says an asserter is <cite index="62-3">expected to defend the claim against legitimate challenges or take it back.</cite>
findings.note: Defence and retraction are central, but as consequences of an act already performed at utterance. This is the synchronic rival the thesis must beat in underdetermined cases.

findings.part: Named target: Butlin & Viebahn's sanctionability requirement (not purely output-time)
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="11-3">An entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and be capable of being sanctioned by agents it interacts with.</cite> The second requirement <cite index="11-4">arises from assertion's nature as a norm-governed social practice.</cite>
findings.note: The abstract treats descriptive function and sanctionability as capacity conditions on the entity. It does not show whether status is fixed at output, so the claim that they hold it synchronic is only partly supported. Sanctioning is inherently after the output, though it is framed as a capacity, not as a later act that fixes an output's status.

findings.part: Named target: Williams & Bayne's proto-assertion treats defence and correction-responsiveness as behavioural evidence
findings.source: Williams & Bayne, "Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion", Inquiry 69(6), 2026 (arXiv 2410.16645)
findings.what_they_say: They note that <cite index="70-3,70-4">adult human assertions typically come with the expectation that the speaker will try to defend them against reasonable challenges.</cite> They say chatbots <cite index="7-7">may be appropriately responsive to correction.</cite>
findings.note: Defending and correcting enter their case only as dispositional features of the system's behavioural profile. Nothing found says that a particular output's status is fixed by that output's later owning, so the synchronic reading is partly confirmed and partly complicated.

findings.part: Named target: Gubelmann holds that speech-act status depends on producer intentions (a producer-state view)
findings.source: Gubelmann, "Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now)", Philosophy & Technology, 2024
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="24-5,24-6">To use language is to act, but LLMs cannot act because they lack intentions.</cite>
findings.note: This confirms the intention-based, producer-state premise the thesis targets. It does not address the timing of when intentions must exist.

findings.part: The claim that all positions ground assertion in speaker-side properties at output
findings.source: "Assertion, Accountability, and Large Language Models" (authors not shown in the result), Philosophy & Technology, 2026
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="22-3">The assumption that assertions must be grounded in the properties of individual speakers does not hold uniformly where non-agentive outputs are taken up within human practices as sources of reasons.</cite>
findings.note: A very recent paper already denies that speaker-grounding is universal, via uptake and function. That weakens 'every position is synchronic and producer-fixed', though it is not the producer's later ownership.

findings.part: Illocutionary force is not uniformly fixed by speaker's intention at the time of speaking
findings.source: Special-issue editorial, "Norms of Public Argument: A Speech Act Perspective", Topoi, 2023
findings.what_they_say: Speech act theory <cite index="33-3">remains vague on how illocutionary force is fixed: via Speaker's intentions, Hearers' uptake, an on-the-fly contract, or external factors.</cite>
findings.note: The field openly treats the fixing of force as unsettled, so 'synchronic producer-state' is not a uniform consensus. Uptake views are about the hearer, not the producer's later owning.

findings.part: Empirical base: people defend and endorse after-the-fact explanations they did not produce from the reasons given, with beliefs and memories shifting toward them
findings.source: Bortolotti et al., "Stranger than Fiction: Costs and Benefits of Everyday Confabulation", PMC, 2018; Johansson et al., choice blindness, 2005–06
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="57-7">In confabulating, a person offers an ill-grounded explanation and also forms the belief that the explanation is true.</cite> In choice blindness, <cite index="55-6">participants offer introspectively derived reasons for choices they did not make.</cite>
findings.note: These show that retroactive endorsement and commitment after confabulation are real, documented human phenomena. They are not about assertion status, so they supply an evidence base and not an anticipation.

finding.what_is_left: In human cases where output-time facts underdetermine the act (blurts, confabulated explanations), the speaker's subsequent owning, defending or retracting is part of what makes the earlier remark an assertion, and not merely evidence of an earlier intention. Conversation analysis and discourse analysis already say later turns retroactively fix or display act-type, and the standard speech-act view treats retraction as a new act that leaves the original act's identity unchanged. So the surviving contribution is the constitutive, commitment-based reading for assertion in underdetermined cases. Extending that to LLMs also needs an argument that a model's defending or retracting is genuine ownership by a persisting commitment-bearer, which a recent 'Diachronic Argument' paper denies. The universal claims that every position is synchronic and that determinate cases are fixed at utterance should be dropped or narrowed.
finding.not_found: I found no source arguing that the producer's own later owning is constitutive of assertoric status for blurts, confabulations or LLM outputs. I also found no work that makes ownership-under-challenge the test for chatbot proto-assertion. That is weak evidence, since most of this is paywalled and my searches were few. I did not search Brandom-style scorekeeping literature, work on retrospective authorship or responsibility for half-conscious speech, or empirical work on attributing assertion after retraction. I did not read the full text of Gubelmann, Butlin & Viebahn or the Williams & Bayne paper beyond abstracts and snippets, so the claim that they 'share a synchronic assumption' is checked only for intention and sanctionability and not exhaustively. I could not verify authorship of the Roulet-style chapter, the 2026 'Assertion, Accountability' paper, or 'Talking with Language Models'. The empirical searches reached conversation analysis and the confabulation and choice-blindness literature, but none was about assertion status. No search on blurts or on speech-act classification by later endorsement was run in psychology or linguistics.

sep.why: The theses concern what makes an utterance an assertion (including chatbot outputs and retroactive ownership), so the entry on assertion is primary, speech-acts is the neighbouring debate about speech-act status and commitment, and artificial-intelligence is the closest candidate for the question of whether chatbot outputs count.

findings.position: Assertion requires explicitness/determinacy of content and force; if the hearer cannot tell what is intended, the utterance fails to be assertoric. This is a determinacy-at-utterance view, which the thesis qualifies but does not directly deny.
findings.who: Fricker (2012); criticized by Hawthorne (2012), Peet (2015, 2021), García-Carpintero (2016, 2019b)
findings.quote: as soon as it is not fully determinate to the hearer what the intended content of an utterance is, or what force it is made with, the utterance fails to be assertoric.
findings.note: The thesis says underdetermined cases are settled later, whereas Fricker says they simply fail to be assertions; a referee would raise this contrast.

findings.position: Commitment accounts tie assertion to what the speaker does after the utterance: defending or retracting when challenged. This gives the thesis ownership/disowning machinery to build on.
findings.quote: To assert a sentence S ... is ( inter alia ) to commit oneself to providing adequate grounds for the truth of S ... One can escape this commitment only by withdrawing the assertion.
findings.note: The entry treats later defence and retraction as part of the commitment structure. It does not claim they settle which act was performed.

findings.position: There is no norm for making assertions at all, only norms on later reactions: defend or retract when challenged. This makes post-utterance conduct central, though to normative status rather than act-type identity.
findings.quote: there is no norm at all for proper making of assertions. There are only norms that govern later reactions.
findings.note: This is close in spirit, since later conduct does the work. But it concerns the normative status of an act already performed.

findings.position: Illocutionary acts do not depend on hearer reaction, only on uptake. Assertion's speaker-content structure makes it less dependent even on uptake. This supports the view that the act is fixed at utterance by speaker-side facts.
findings.quote: The illocutionary act does not depend on the hearer's reaction to the utterance.
findings.note: Mild pressure on any view that lets later events fix the act. It concerns hearer reaction, not the speaker's own later avowal.

findings.position: Defeasible surface features of declarative sentences, with default speaker and hearer patterns, characterize assertion. Departures such as lying or a distrustful hearer are allowed.
findings.quote: it is the cognitive patterns associated with surface features, on the production and comprehension sides, that characterize assertion.
findings.note: Gives a utterance-time default that later ownership could override or confirm in non-default cases.

findings.position: Sneaky or underdetermined assertions and indirect assertion raise the question of whether content not exactly expressed still counts as assertion proper.
findings.quote: One question is whether an utterance is an assertion proper that p if that content is not exactly what is expressed
findings.note: Related borderline cases, but the entry settles them by content and force, not by later owning.

findings.position: Intention-based accounts make the act depend on speaker intentions. Questions are raised about whether the speaker must intend it to be an assertion or make it voluntarily. This bears on blurts.
findings.quote: must he intend it to be an assertion? Must it be made voluntarily?
findings.note: The entry raises the voluntariness question for blurts only in passing and leaves it open.

nearest_positions: Determinacy requirement: underdetermined force or content means no assertion — Fricker (2012), opposed by Hawthorne, Peet, García-Carpintero
Commitment/accountability accounts: defend or retract on challenge — Brandom, MacFarlane, Peirce, Alston, Rescorla
Pagin's prima facie informativeness account, with defeasible default patterns tied to surface features
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Chatbot or machine outputs, blurts, and confabulations are not discussed. The entry also never says that a speaker's retrospective owning or disowning determines which speech act was performed. It treats retraction and defence as commitment-discharging, not act-individuating.

findings.position: Retraction/withdrawal is a post-hoc act available for speech acts. The entry treats later retraction as something one can do to a speech act already performed, with commitments dissolving. This is a resource for a thesis about later owning/disowning, though the entry says retraction does not change which act was performed.
findings.quote: on Wednesday I may be able to retract a claim I made on Monday... In both these cases of assertion and promise, I am now no longer beholden to the commitments that the speech acts engender in spite of the fact that the past is fixed.
findings.note: Retraction is distinguished from changing the past; the thesis claims later owning helps settle which act was performed, which goes beyond retraction.

findings.position: Whether an act was performed is fixed by the speaker's intentions and overt commitment at the time of utterance. Force is an aspect of speaker meaning, so later attitudes are not constitutive of the act.
findings.quote: We perform a speech act, then, when we overtly commit ourselves in a certain way to a content
findings.note: The entry's accounts make the act depend on utterance-time intention and manifest commitment, so later owning would be evidence at most, not a settler.

findings.position: Force is underdetermined by content, mood and the observable utterance itself, so the question of which act was performed can remain open. The entry also has the speaker's intention as decisive and discernible only through contextual cues.
findings.quote: the communicative significance of an act may be underdetermined by what has been said or observably done.
findings.note: Gives the underdetermination premise the thesis starts from.

findings.position: Intention is required for speech acts, yet efficacy requires more than intending. Speech acts need an intentional undertaking of a publicly accessible commitment, which bears on blurts and non-intentional outputs (no intention, no act).
findings.quote: speech acts involve intentional undertaking of a publicly accessible commitment; further, that commitment is not undertaken simply by virtue of my intending to undertake it
findings.note: A referee will ask whether blurts and confabulations have any such undertaking at output time.

findings.position: The somniloquist and joker/actor cases show that an utterance's form does not suffice for a speech act. Uptake can also be required for some acts, so audience response, rather than speaker avowal, can co-determine whether an act succeeded.
findings.quote: while talking in my sleep I might say, “I hereby promise to climb the Eiffel Tower,” without thereby making any promise.
findings.note: Related non-assertion cases; the entry attributes the failure to missing intention/commitment, not to later disowning.

findings.position: Uptake and addressee responses can determine whether an act is performed at all (misfire), so post-utterance facts sometimes matter. But these are audience facts, not speaker owning.
findings.quote: If you do not accept that bet, then I have tried to bet but have not succeeded in betting.
findings.note: Nearest precedent for post-utterance facts bearing on act identity, though it concerns the hearer and not the speaker.

findings.position: Assertion carries commitment to defend the content, and one is obliged to retract if unable to meet the challenge. This links assertoric status to how the speaker later responds to challenges.
findings.quote: she is obliged to retract P if she is unable to respond to that challenge adequately.
findings.note: Provides the normative route by which later owning/disowning could matter.

nearest_positions: Force as overtly manifested commitment at utterance (speaker meaning) — Green; Strawson 1964 intentionalism
Retraction/withdrawal as post-hoc act that leaves the past act intact — Sbisà 2007
Uptake as a condition of success for some speech acts — Austin; Langton; Hornsby and Langton (contra Bird 2002)
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: The entry says nothing about blurts, confabulation, or chatbot/LLM outputs, nor about whether later owning or disowning by a speaker retroactively fixes which speech act was performed. It does not discuss the idea of a determinate/indeterminate split.

findings.position: The Turing Test operationalizes linguistic indistinguishability as the criterion for machine linguistic competence, which is about outputs and behavior rather than which speech act was performed. The entry never asks whether a machine's output counts as an assertion.
findings.who: Turing (1950); Nilsson (1998) defines AI by it
findings.quote: Passing in this sense operationalizes linguistic indistinguishability.
findings.note: A referee would ask whether chatbot outputs count as assertions at all; the entry treats only behavioral indistinguishability.

findings.position: Descartes' test says machines could utter words and emit canned responses but could never arrange speech to reply appropriately to everything said. This is a different criterion from the act-type question, but it bears on whether machine utterances are genuine speech acts.
findings.quote: it never happens that it arranges its speech in various ways, in order to reply appropriately to everything that may be said in its presence
findings.note: Denies machine speech the status of genuine linguistic acts on grounds of flexibility, not retrospective ownership.

findings.position: Weak versus strong AI and the Chinese Room: whether machine symbol output has understanding or intentionality. This is the nearest place the entry would locate the question of whether a chatbot output is an assertion.
findings.who: Searle (Chinese Room), discussed in section 8.2 (only listed in the table of contents; the text is cut off before it)
findings.quote: 8.2 The Chinese Room Argument Against “Strong AI”
findings.note: The entry text is truncated, so the argument itself is not quotable; only the section heading is visible.

findings.position: Machines can have a theory of mind and be built to lie, which makes the assertion versus non-assertion distinction for machine outputs a live question. A lying machine presupposes outputs that can be sincere or insincere.
findings.quote: Clark (2010) uses a computational theory of the mind, the ability to represent and reason about other agents, to build a lying machine that successfully persuades people into believing falsehoods.
findings.note: Gives a hook for chatbot outputs being treated as assertions, but nothing on later owning or disowning.

nearest_positions: Turing Test as behavioral operationalization of linguistic competence — Turing 1950; Nilsson 1998
Descartes' language test: machine speech lacks flexible, appropriate response, so it is not genuine speech — Descartes 1637
Chinese Room / strong vs. weak AI on whether machine symbol output has understanding or intentionality — Searle (heading only in the entry)
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Speech-act theory, assertion, blurts, confabulation, retrospective owning or disowning of utterances, and whether an act's type is fixed at utterance or settled by later commitment. The entry does not discuss any of these, and it never treats chatbot outputs as candidate assertions.

theses: Where output-time facts underdetermine whether a remark was an assertion (blurts, confabulations, and possibly chatbot outputs), the speaker's later owning or disowning helps settle which act was performed. Determinate cases are fixed at utterance.
